html:
The Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) runs an oil pipeline about 1,500 km long from the Tengiz field in western Kazakhstan, around the north of the Caspian Sea, to a terminal near Novorossiysk on Russia's Black Sea coast. It opened in 2001 and carries almost all of Kazakhstan's oil exports, about one percent of the world's oil supply.

The consortium joins Russian and Kazakh state companies with Western oil firms such as Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell. It was built because Kazakhstan, landlocked, had no route of its own to world markets after 1991, and the old Soviet pipelines all ran through Russia. Oil from Tengiz, Karachaganak and Kashagan flows through it, and that money paid for much of the new capital and moves the value of the tenge.

The route through Russia is also its weak point. Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Russian courts and inspectors have halted loading several times, and Ukrainian drones have struck its pumping stations. Kazakhstan has looked for other routes, across the Caspian to Baku.
